subject: WAIC and a structural time-series model

messages.author: 0c7ffcac30445989
messages.subject: WAIC and a structural time-series model
parts:
Hi All,

When Nimble calculates the WAIC for a given mcmc/model, how does it determine what parameters to sample if the observations are not totally independent? 

In my case, I've built a structural time-series model and each observation is dependent on the previous one AND the various latent parameters in the model. I was thinking about altering the WAIC to account for that temporal structure, but then I started wondering how Nimble calculates the WAIC. If it uses the relationships in the graph of the model to determine what needs to be sampled as a parameter, then I'm wondering whether it's already including the previous observation in the parameter vector for the posterior prediction. If so, then I might not need to do anything differently and I could maybe argue that Nimble has dealt with the dependence for me. If not, and Nimble only uses the strictly latent nodes as parameters for WAIC, then I'll probably have to think more carefully about my adjustment to WAIC and write my own function to estimate it given the mcmc posterior samples.

Any thought here would be greatly appreciated.

Chris

messages.author: 8d776ea00a3d5b38
messages.subject: Re: WAIC and a structural time-series model
parts:
(Forgot to post this to nimble-users!)

Hi Chris, 

Here's a little bit more detail on NIMBLE's WAIC procedure:

1)  The WAIC algorithm iterates over the posterior samples that have been obtained by the MCMC algorithm.  For each set of posterior samples, these sampled posterior values are inserted into the model.  To see which parameters are being inserted into the model, you can check the column names of as.matrix(mcmc$mvSamples).  

2)  For each of these posterior samples that have been inserted into the model, new values for every stochastic, non-data node that depends on these sampled nodes are then simulated conditional upon the set of posterior values that have been inserted into the model.  

3)  The probabilities for each of the data nodes in the model are then calculated, conditioned upon the posterior values of the nodes sampled by the mcmc algorithm and the simulated values of any other stochastic downstream nodes.  

These three steps repeat for each of the posterior samples that were obtained by the MCMC, and then the WAIC is calculated using all of the data node probabilities obtained in step 3.  

I'm not sure if this will make anything clearer, but here's an example using a simple time series model:

sigmaX ~ dunif(0, 10)  ##  sigmaX is an unknown parameter
x[1] ~ dnorm(0, sigmaX)
y[1] ~ dnorm(x[1], 1)
for(t in 2:T){
  x[t] ~ dnorm(x[t-1], sigmaX)  ## x[t] is a latent state at time t, depends on x[t-1]
  y[t] ~ dnorm(x[t], 1)  ## y[t] is the observed data at time t
}

If we run an MCMC on the above model and get posterior samples for sigmaX, then the WAIC algorithm will proceed by, for each posterior sample for sigmaX:

- simulating data values for x[1], ... x[T] given that posterior value of sigmaX
- calculating probabilities p( y[t] | x[t] ) for t = 1, ... T, given the newly simulated x[t] values

I'm not totally sure whether this description gives an answer to your question or not - if not, or if you have any other questions, definitely let me know and I'd be happy to think more carefully about the problem.  Additionally, if you do decide to code your own WAIC function, the source code for NIMBLE's WAIC calculation can be found here (starting on line 147):

https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble/blob/devel/packages/nimble/R/MCMC_build.R

Possibly looking at that code could help when you're writing a customized WAIC.

Thanks!

Nick

Hi Nick,

Thanks very much for the response. Your description was clear and it helped!

I should probably make a formal feature request on GitHub or something, but it would be nice to add options for WAIC like those presented in Gelmen et al. 2013 (Bayesian Data Analysis) pg. 173 where they include a scaling constant and two different formulations of WAIC—one for the mean and the other for variance of individual terms. Might be nice to have those options at some future time.

Best,

C
